discovery.question: A mining company offers a tribal district roads, schools and jobs. The Gram Sabha rejects it to protect their forest and way of life. Who understands 'development' correctly?
options: Both — development means different things to different people, and their goals can genuinely clash
Only the company — roads and jobs are real development, forests are sentimental
Only the Gram Sabha — development always means refusing industry
Neither — development has one fixed definition that settles this
discovery.answer: Both — development means different things to different people, and their goals can genuinely clash
discovery.hook: There is no single scoreboard for a good life. A wage, a forest, a safe walk to school — what counts as 'developed' depends on whose life you're measuring.

c10_eco_ch01.mission: Interview four people in a village — a landless labourer, a farmer, a schoolgirl, a factory owner — and prove their versions of 'development' can't all be bought with the same rupee.
c10_eco_ch01.finale: Income is a means, not the destination. Real development is a bundle of goals — freedom, equality, security — that sometimes even collide with each other.
c10_eco_ch01.subtitle: Discover why 'a better life' means different things to different people
c10_eco_ch01.role: a panchayat advisor deciding how to spend a development fund
c10_eco_ch01.intro: A district gets money for exactly one project — a watershed, a skill centre, or a cold storage. Every group in the village wants a different one, and each has a point.
c10_eco_ch01.goal: Explain that development goals vary and conflict, and separate income goals from freedom, equality and security.

discovery.question: A sugar mill buys sugarcane straight from farmers. Since it works on a primary-sector crop, the mill must be primary sector too — right?
options: Wrong — the mill transforms cane into sugar, so it's secondary; it's the output, not the input, that decides the sector
Right — anything using farm produce stays in the primary sector
It's tertiary — because the mill also sells the sugar
It splits — half primary for crushing, half secondary for packing
discovery.answer: Wrong — the mill transforms cane into sugar, so it's secondary; it's the output, not the input, that decides the sector
discovery.hook: Don't classify a job by what goes in — classify it by what comes out. Nature's gift is primary, a transformed thing is secondary, a service is tertiary.

c10_eco_ch02.mission: Trace one litre of milk from a cow in a village to a chilled packet in a city store — tag every stage primary, secondary or tertiary — then explain why services rule India's GDP but not its jobs.
c10_eco_ch02.finale: Wheat to flour to a delivered pizza: one grain, three sectors. India's puzzle is that the sector earning the most isn't the one employing the most.
c10_eco_ch02.subtitle: Sort the whole economy into three buckets — then find the imbalance
c10_eco_ch02.role: an economist mapping India's production chain
c10_eco_ch02.intro: Your grandfather's village grows the wheat; a mill grinds it; a delivery app brings the pizza. Every rupee you spend lands in one of three sectors.
c10_eco_ch02.goal: Classify activities by nature of output and analyse why tertiary leads GDP while primary still leads employment.

discovery.question: A wheat farmer needs shoes. In a barter world, what must happen before he can trade?
options: He must find a shoemaker who wants wheat, in the right amount, right now — a double coincidence of wants
He just needs to find any shoemaker with his shoe size
He needs the government to fix a wheat-for-shoes rate
Nothing special — barter works exactly like money
discovery.answer: He must find a shoemaker who wants wheat, in the right amount, right now — a double coincidence of wants
discovery.hook: Barter doesn't just make trade awkward — it makes whole industries impossible. Money's real job is letting you sell to one person and buy from another.

c10_eco_ch03.mission: Sell 50 kg of tomatoes, survive a barter nightmare, then track your own salary through cash, UPI and deposits to see what actually counts as 'money.'
c10_eco_ch03.finale: A ₹500 note and a UPI balance are both money — one printed and guaranteed, the other a promise your bank keeps on demand. Money is trust you can spend.
c10_eco_ch03.subtitle: From barter chaos to UPI — what makes money, money
c10_eco_ch03.role: a village trader trying to escape the barter trap
c10_eco_ch03.intro: In a remote haat, a trader can't sell his cloth because the farmers don't want what he brought. One invention would fix it — and you carry it in your pocket.
c10_eco_ch03.goal: Explain double coincidence of wants, and treat demand deposits as real money alongside currency.

discovery.question: Your phone was 'assembled in India' — yet its processor was designed in the USA, chips came from Korea, the screen from China. So which country actually made your phone?
options: No single country — a global production chain splits each stage wherever it's cheapest or most skilled
China — because most parts shipped from there
India — because final assembly is where a product is 'made'
The USA — because the company that designed it is American
discovery.answer: No single country — a global production chain splits each stage wherever it's cheapest or most skilled
discovery.hook: Globalisation isn't about importing finished goods — it's about slicing one product across the planet so each piece is made where it makes most sense.

c10_eco_ch04.mission: Follow an electric scooter's battery, body and assembly across three countries, compute the landed cost of imported wheat, and judge who wins when markets integrate.
c10_eco_ch04.finale: One product, many passports. MNCs stitch the world into a single factory — and the fight is over who captures the value and who gets just the wages.
c10_eco_ch04.subtitle: Unpick the global journey of the products in your pocket
c10_eco_ch04.role: a trade analyst mapping where products really come from
c10_eco_ch04.intro: Samsung, Apple, Xiaomi and Lava all fight for space on one Indian shelf — a sight impossible when import duties topped 100% and two car models ruled the roads.
c10_eco_ch04.goal: Explain global production chains and market integration, including why prices converge but never fully equalise.

discovery.question: A ₹500 'pure ghee' packet turns out adulterated. The shopkeeper blames the company, the company ignores your letter, and a lawyer costs more than the ghee. What does this prove?
options: Individual buyers are too weak to fight alone — that's exactly why a consumer movement had to be organised
Nothing — cheating on small purchases is just part of shopping
Only expensive products deserve legal protection
The consumer should simply stop buying branded goods
discovery.answer: Individual buyers are too weak to fight alone — that's exactly why a consumer movement had to be organised
discovery.hook: One cheated buyer is a nuisance; a movement is a force. The rights you now take for granted were won by two decades of testing, exposing and organising.

c10_eco_ch05.mission: Take a burst pressure cooker with no ISI mark and no refund to the District Forum — identify every right violated and argue for the relief a consumer deserves.
c10_eco_ch05.finale: Safety, information, choice, redressal — four rights that turned 'buyer beware' into 'seller, be fair.' The movement started long before the law caught up.
c10_eco_ch05.subtitle: Turn a bad purchase into a case the law must answer
c10_eco_ch05.role: a consumer-rights advocate arguing before a district forum
c10_eco_ch05.intro: A pressure cooker lid bursts on first use — no instructions, no ISI mark, no refund. What sounds like bad luck is actually four legal violations at once.
c10_eco_ch05.goal: Name the consumer rights, trace the movement that won them, and apply them to real complaints.

discovery.question: Lencho's crops are destroyed, so he writes a letter addressed simply 'To God' demanding 100 pesos. When the post office staff collect 70 and send it, he's angry — not grateful. What does his anger reveal?
options: His faith was so literal he believed God sent the full amount — and the post office 'stole' the rest
He's ungrateful — 70 pesos should have been enough
He realised too late that writing to God was foolish
He was angry the letter took so long to deliver
discovery.answer: His faith was so literal he believed God sent the full amount — and the post office 'stole' the rest
discovery.hook: Lencho isn't a fool — he's a man with no bank, no insurance, no helpline. When no human institution will help, absolute faith in God is the only plan left.

c10_engl_ch01.mission: Reread the hailstorm scene and hunt the imagery — 'frozen pearls,' a field 'white as if covered with salt' — then build a PEEL answer on what Lencho's faith really is.
c10_engl_ch01.finale: The story's deepest irony: the people who answered his letter proved his faith in God — while he accused them of robbing him. Faith and irony share one envelope.
c10_engl_ch01.subtitle: Read a letter to God and the irony of the humans who answered it
c10_engl_ch01.role: a literary detective decoding what a farmer's letter really means
c10_engl_ch01.intro: A farmer loses everything to one hour of hail, and his solution is a stamp, a pen and an address no post office can deliver.
c10_engl_ch01.goal: Analyse Lencho's faith as literal and transactional, and support every claim with textual evidence.

discovery.question: At Mandela's 1994 inauguration, the military generals who once would have arrested him now saluted him — and two national anthems played, one for each community. Why sing BOTH anthems?
options: It was a deliberate act of reconciliation — no group's identity was erased in the new nation
It was just ceremony — extra songs to fill the program
The organisers couldn't decide which anthem to keep
One anthem was for Mandela, the other for the outgoing president
discovery.answer: It was a deliberate act of reconciliation — no group's identity was erased in the new nation
discovery.hook: That day wasn't only about one man's freedom — it was a whole country performing a new idea: that the oppressor and the oppressed could belong to the same anthem.

c10_engl_ch02.mission: Reconstruct the machinery of apartheid — the acts that assigned race, controlled movement, and dictated where people could exist — then weigh what the inauguration dismantled.
c10_engl_ch02.finale: Apartheid wasn't just separate benches; it was a legal machine that defined who you were at birth. Freedom meant dismantling the machine, not just opening the benches.
c10_engl_ch02.subtitle: Walk out of apartheid's cage into a rainbow nation's first morning
c10_engl_ch02.role: a journalist covering 10 May 1994 at the Union Buildings
c10_engl_ch02.intro: For decades your skin decided your school, your bench, your bus. On one May morning in Pretoria, that entire system bowed to a man it had imprisoned for 27 years.
c10_engl_ch02.goal: Explain apartheid as a legal-bureaucratic system and read the inauguration as a national ritual of reconciliation.

discovery.question: The young seagull's mother flies up with a piece of fish — then halts mid-air, just out of his reach. Starving, he dives at the fish and finds himself flying. Was the family abandoning him all along?
options: No — they staged a controlled crisis: withholding food, circling, calling, until hunger beat fear
Yes — they gave up on him and left him to survive or starve
No — the mother simply couldn't land on the narrow ledge
Partly — they abandoned him but came back when they heard him cry
discovery.answer: No — they staged a controlled crisis: withholding food, circling, calling, until hunger beat fear
discovery.hook: The first flight wasn't bravery — it was engineering. His family built a situation where staying afraid cost more than jumping.

c10_engl_ch03.mission: Track every detail the author plants — the mocking siblings, the hunger, the mother hovering with fish — and argue whether the seagull conquered fear or fear was outmanoeuvred.
c10_engl_ch03.finale: Sometimes the only way past a ledge is a push you don't recognise as love. Hunger did what courage couldn't — and the sea caught him gently.
c10_engl_ch03.subtitle: Watch a terrified seagull get tricked into his first flight
c10_engl_ch03.role: a behavioural scientist reading a bird family's strategy
c10_engl_ch03.intro: His brothers and sister flew days ago. He watches from the ledge, pretending to sleep, too scared to try — until his mother weaponises his own stomach.
c10_engl_ch03.goal: Analyse fear as layered psychology and support claims about the family's deliberate staging with evidence.

discovery.question: Anne Frank writes 'Dear Kitty' instead of 'Dear Diary,' and says 'paper has more patience than people.' In a sealed-off annex, what is the diary actually doing for her?
options: It's a survival tool — writing builds her a confidante and a self that the Nazis were trying to erase
It's a teenage phase — she's just a normal lonely girl who wants a friend
It's homework — she planned to publish it as a book someday
It's evidence — she was recording Nazi crimes for a future trial
discovery.answer: It's a survival tool — writing builds her a confidante and a self that the Nazis were trying to erase
discovery.hook: When a regime strips you of your school, your tram, your park bench — writing 'I still exist' onto a page is not a hobby. It's resistance.

c10_engl_ch04.mission: Place a 13-year-old's diary inside its history — trace the laws that caged her life — then prove why 'lonely teenager' is a one-mark answer, not a three-mark one.
c10_engl_ch04.finale: The Holocaust isn't background to the diary — it's the lens for every entry. Anne wrote in real time, not knowing the ending, which is exactly why we can't stop reading.
c10_engl_ch04.subtitle: Meet the girl who turned a notebook into a lifeline
c10_engl_ch04.role: a historian reading a real-time document of the Holocaust
c10_engl_ch04.intro: Forbidden from trams, schools and park benches at thirteen, a girl in hiding names her diary and tells it everything she cannot tell a soul.
c10_engl_ch04.goal: Connect the diary to Holocaust history and explain Kitty as confidante, not literary device.

discovery.question: In a Goan village, a man in a knee-length kabai arrives each morning to the 'jhang-jhang' of a bamboo staff — and the text insists he is NOT a relic of the past. What is he really?
options: A living cultural institution — his breads are still essential to every Goan festival and marriage
A quaint historical figure — the last of the old Portuguese bakers
Just a bread-seller doing his morning and evening rounds
A tourist attraction maintained for nostalgia
discovery.answer: A living cultural institution — his breads are still essential to every Goan festival and marriage
discovery.hook: The pader didn't survive as a museum piece. Bol at Christmas, sandwiches at engagements — Goa took a Portuguese import and made it impossible to celebrate without.

c10_engl_ch05.mission: Follow the baker's daily route through the village — his kabai, his furnace, his jhang-jhang — and show how a colonial legacy became a Goan necessity.
c10_engl_ch05.finale: Culture isn't what invaders leave behind; it's what people choose to keep. The pader endures because Goa kneaded Portuguese bread into its own identity.
c10_engl_ch05.subtitle: Hear the jhang-jhang that still runs a Goan village's mornings
c10_engl_ch05.role: a food historian tracing how bread became Goan
c10_engl_ch05.intro: Before alarm clocks, a bamboo staff's rhythm told a Goan village that morning — and fresh pao — had arrived.
c10_engl_ch05.goal: Explain the Portuguese legacy in Goan baking and why the pader is a cultural institution, not a vendor.

discovery.question: After his dog Jonnie dies, Maxwell doesn't get another dog — he imports an otter from Iraq. A classmate says: 'He was lonely and otters are cute.' What's missing from that reading?
options: A deliberate chain of reasoning — grief, rejecting a replacement dog, a childhood fascination, and a cottage ringed by water fit for an otter
Nothing — loneliness fully explains an impulse purchase
Money — only a rich man could order an otter
Luck — an otter happened to be available nearby
discovery.answer: A deliberate chain of reasoning — grief, rejecting a replacement dog, a childhood fascination, and a cottage ringed by water fit for an otter
discovery.hook: Mijbil wasn't a whim; he was a decision with steps. And his settling in wasn't a straight line — joy one day, panic the next, like any wild thing learning a house.

c10_engl_ch06.mission: Chart Mijbil's first days — the hiding, the bathroom experiments, the glorious chaos in water — and show why 'he adapted quickly' only earns half the marks.
c10_engl_ch06.finale: A wild animal doesn't 'settle'; it negotiates. Maxwell's patience and Mijbil's zig-zag trust are the real story of two species learning each other.
c10_engl_ch06.subtitle: Track an otter's zig-zag road from Iraqi marshes to a Scottish home
c10_engl_ch06.role: an animal behaviourist observing a wild otter indoors
c10_engl_ch06.intro: A remote cottage by the water, a man grieving his dog, and a parcel from Iraq containing something that would turn bathtubs into playgrounds.
c10_engl_ch06.goal: Trace Maxwell's decision-making and Mijbil's non-linear adaptation using concrete behavioural evidence.

discovery.question: Eight-year-old Valli rides the bus to town and back — alone. She never does chores for cash, never asks the conductor directly. So how did she pull it off?
options: Months of resisting peppermints and toys to save sixty paise — plus fare and timing details lifted from eavesdropping
She saved gift money and boldly questioned the driver about the route
She snuck aboard while the conductor was distracted
Her mother secretly funded the trip as a surprise
discovery.answer: Months of resisting peppermints and toys to save sixty paise — plus fare and timing details lifted from eavesdropping
discovery.hook: This isn't childish daydreaming — it's a project. Every coin refused, every adult conversation mined for clues. Valli planned her ride like a heist.

c10_engl_ch07.mission: Piece together Valli's intelligence operation — what she overheard, what she sacrificed, what she refused — then write the case for her 'tiny wish' being iron will.
c10_engl_ch07.finale: The bus was never the point — the self-control was. An eight-year-old who can resist a hundred peppermints can get almost anywhere.
c10_engl_ch07.subtitle: Follow an eight-year-old's master plan for one bus ride
c10_engl_ch07.role: a biographer reconstructing how a child out-planned the adults
c10_engl_ch07.intro: Every day a bright bus roars past Valli's house toward a town she's never seen. Most kids would whine for a ride. Valli starts gathering intelligence instead.
c10_engl_ch07.goal: Show how the author builds character through indirect detail — observation, sacrifice, discretion — not just plot.

discovery.question: Kisa Gotami carries her dead son door to door begging for medicine. The neighbours say she's lost her senses. Are they being cruel — or seeing something she can't?
options: They're seeing grief's blindness — her love is so total it overrides the plain fact that he's gone
They're cruel — a good neighbour would search for the medicine with her
Neither — they simply didn't have any medicine to give
They're afraid — her grief might be contagious
discovery.answer: They're seeing grief's blindness — her love is so total it overrides the plain fact that he's gone
discovery.hook: The parable doesn't mock her — it honours her. Buddha's cure isn't medicine for the boy; it's a lesson that lets a shattered mother finally set him down.

c10_engl_ch08.mission: Trace Siddhartha's road from palace to the Bodhi tree — and don't mix up the Four Sights with the Four Noble Truths — then follow Kisa Gotami's mustard-seed journey.
c10_engl_ch08.finale: Every door she knocked had buried someone. That's the sermon without words: grief is universal, and accepting impermanence is the only medicine that exists.
c10_engl_ch08.subtitle: Walk from a prince's palace to a mother's unbearable lesson
c10_engl_ch08.role: a student of Buddha decoding a 2,500-year-old teaching
c10_engl_ch08.intro: A sheltered prince sees an old man, a sick man, a corpse and a monk — and abandons a kingdom. Years later, a grieving mother brings him her impossible request.
c10_engl_ch08.goal: Sequence the Buddha's transformation and interpret the mustard-seed parable as a lesson in universal mortality.

discovery.question: Lomov visits his neighbour to propose marriage — and the play ends with the 'engaged' couple screaming about whose dog is superior. What is Chekhov actually satirising?
options: People who prize winning arguments and property over the very marriage they're arranging
Romantic love — the play says all proposals end badly
Bad manners — the characters just needed etiquette lessons
Dogs — the real subject is which breed is best
discovery.answer: People who prize winning arguments and property over the very marriage they're arranging
discovery.hook: The proposal is bait, not the point. Chekhov makes the meadows worthless and the evidence vague on purpose — so you watch pride detonate over absolutely nothing.

c10_engl_ch09.mission: Dissect the Oxen Meadows quarrel line by line: find every ownership claim, notice how worthless the prize is, and explain why the argument is funniest precisely because it's pointless.
c10_engl_ch09.finale: A marriage proposal derailed by meadows and dogs isn't a rom-com — it's a farce holding up a mirror: watch what people fight for when nobody's watching their dignity.
c10_engl_ch09.subtitle: Watch a marriage proposal get demolished by a land dispute
c10_engl_ch09.role: a theatre critic reviewing a farce that refuses to be romantic
c10_engl_ch09.intro: A man in evening dress comes to propose. Before he can finish, he and the bride-to-be are shouting about a strip of land worth almost nothing.
c10_engl_ch09.goal: Identify the farce genre, analyse the Oxen Meadows argument, and correct the 'romantic comedy' misreading.
